intro: A pinch of salt dissolves in water and disappears. A pencil mark, a diamond and the graphite bricks of the first nuclear reactor are all the same element, carbon. A hand warmer heats itself, a cold pack chills itself, and neither is plugged in. A piece of ancient charcoal from an Illinois riverbank can tell you how long ago the fire went out. Every one of these is a question about matter: what it is made of, how its pieces hold together, and what happens when they change partners.

This unit starts inside the atom, with three particles and a set of rules about how electrons arrange themselves. Those rules explain the periodic table, the chart that let Dmitri Mendeleev predict elements no one had found. They explain why metals conduct and bend, why salts shatter and dissolve, and why one form of carbon writes on paper while another cuts glass. Then the unit turns to change: how atoms rearrange in a reaction, why mass never disappears, where the heat of a fire comes from, and how fast or how far a reaction goes.

The last part reaches the nucleus, which chemistry never touches but physics can. There you will find radioactive decay and the clocks it provides, the splitting of uranium that first sustained itself under a Chicago football stadium in 1942, and the fusion that lights the sun. By the end you should be able to look at a material or a reaction and reason, from evidence, about what its atoms are doing and what will happen next.
bigQuestion: How does the invisible structure of atoms explain the properties of materials and the changes they undergo?

timeline.t: Antoine Lavoisier publishes a textbook stating that mass is conserved in every chemical change
John Dalton proposes that each element is made of its own kind of atom, and that atoms combine in fixed ratios
Dmitri Mendeleev arranges the elements in a periodic table and leaves gaps for elements not yet found
Clemens Winkler discovers germanium, matching Mendeleev's prediction for eka-silicon
Henri Becquerel finds that uranium fogs a photographic plate on its own: radioactivity
J. J. Thomson shows that cathode rays are tiny negative particles, the electron
Ernest Rutherford explains the gold-foil results: the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus
Niels Bohr proposes electron energy levels; Henry Moseley orders the elements by atomic number
Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann split uranium; Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explain and name fission
Enrico Fermi's team achieves the first self-sustaining chain reaction under Stagg Field in Chicago
Willard Libby at the University of Chicago dates ancient wood with carbon-14

words.d: the number of protons in an atom's nucleus, which decides which element it is
an atom of an element with a particular number of neutrons; isotopes differ in mass, not chemistry
an electron in the outermost energy level; valence electrons take part in bonding
the chart of elements arranged by atomic number so that elements with similar behavior line up in columns
the energy needed to remove one electron from an atom
the attraction between positive and negative ions formed when a metal gives electrons to a nonmetal
a bond in which two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons
the attraction between positive metal ions and the free electrons that move among them
the rule that the total mass of the products of a chemical reaction equals the total mass of the reactants
describes a reaction that releases more energy than it absorbs, usually as heat
the time it takes for half the atoms of a radioactive isotope in a sample to decay
the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two smaller nuclei, releasing neutrons and energy

test.q: An atom has 8 protons, 10 neutrons and 8 electrons. Which is true?
choices: It is oxygen-18 with a negative charge
test.why: 8 protons is oxygen; 8 + 10 = 18 is the mass number; equal protons and electrons make it neutral.

test.q: Why did Mendeleev's table become trusted as a scientific tool?
choices: It listed every known element alphabetically
It correctly predicted the properties of elements found later
It was the first list of elements
It ordered elements by their color
test.why: Gallium, scandium and germanium matched the properties he predicted for the gaps.

test.q: Elements in the same group of the periodic table behave alike because they have the same:
test.why: Valence electrons control bonding, and a group shares the same count.

test.q: Which element has the largest atomic radius?
test.why: Atoms grow down a group and shrink across a period; cesium is at the lower left.

test.q: Sodium gives one electron to chlorine. The result is:
choices: A positive ion and a negative ion that attract each other
test.why: Electron transfer makes ions; their attraction is an ionic bond.

test.q: Which property is explained by the sea-of-electrons model of metals?
test.why: Free-moving electrons carry current; the same model explains bending and shine.

test.q: Diamond is hard and graphite is soft, though both are carbon. Why?
choices: They are bonded in different arrangements: a rigid 3-D network versus sliding sheets
test.why: Structure and bonding, not the element, set the properties.

test.q: Aluminum ions are 3+ and oxide ions are 2-. The formula for aluminum oxide is:
A sealed flask of reactants is weighed before and after a reaction that produces gas. The mass:
choices: Stays the same because atoms are only rearranged
test.why: Conservation of mass: nothing leaves the sealed flask, and no atoms are created or destroyed.

test.q: Which coefficient set balances the burning of methane: CH4 + O2 → CO2 + H2O?
test.why: CH4 + 2 O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O gives one carbon, four hydrogens and four oxygens on each side.

test.q: A student wants a reaction to go faster. Which will NOT help?
choices: Grinding a solid reactant to powder
test.why: Cooling slows particles and reduces effective collisions; the other three all increase the rate.

test.q: An instant cold pack gets cold when squeezed. The process inside is:
test.why: It absorbs heat from its surroundings, which is the definition of endothermic.

test.q: A sample of a radioactive isotope has a half-life of 8 days. After 24 days, what fraction remains?
What was the role of graphite in Chicago Pile-1?
choices: It was the fuel that split
It absorbed neutrons to stop the reaction
It slowed neutrons so uranium-235 could capture them
test.why: Graphite was the moderator; cadmium rods were the absorbers and uranium was the fuel.

test.q: Which is the fairest summary of the evidence on nuclear power?
choices: It is steady and low-carbon but leaves long-lived waste and carries rare, severe accident risks
It is completely safe and produces no waste
It is more dangerous than every other energy source
It emits more carbon dioxide than coal
test.why: Both the benefits and the risks are well documented; a fair summary states both.

write.prompt: Should Illinois keep relying on nuclear power for roughly half of its electricity over the next 30 years? Make a claim and support it with evidence from this unit about fission, half-lives, energy in reactions and the trade-offs among energy sources.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence: keep, expand, reduce or replace nuclear power in Illinois.
Use at least three pieces of evidence: how fission releases energy, why spent fuel stays hazardous (half-life), what the plant emits while running, and the comparison with coal, gas, wind and solar.
Explain your reasoning: why does that evidence support your claim rather than the opposite one?
Give the strongest point on the other side and respond to it honestly with evidence, not dismissal.
Say which values tip your decision, since people weighing the same evidence can reach different conclusions.
